transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. It's really nice to meet you, and thank you so much for taking the time to see me. I hope I'm not making a mountain out of a molehill here, I know you're very busy. 

But, um... I guess what brings me in is just this... this feeling I've been having. It's honestly a little embarrassing to talk about, a man my age having this issue, but... well, whenever I'm supposed to just sit quietly—like during our morning staff meetings at the building, or when we have briefings for church events—I get this feeling like I've got a little motor humming right under my skin. 

I really try not to be a bother or be disruptive to anyone, I promise. But I just end up shifting around in my chair a lot, or standing up in the back of the room, or I'll just find some excuse to go move around, like saying I need to check the supply closet. 

Is that... does that make sense to bring up? I just want to make sure I'm explaining it right for you.
Have you started or changed the dose of any new medications recently, particularly anything prescribed for mood, anxiety, or other psychiatric symptoms?

Oh, no, doctor. No, I haven't started anything new at all. Um, I don't take any medications for my mood or anxiety or anything like that. I try to just... well, I try to manage things on my own, you know? Keep a positive attitude and not be a burden. 

So, no new prescriptions or dose changes or anything. Just maybe a regular aspirin now and then if my joints are acting up from mopping the floors, but that's it. I hope that's alright? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Did you notice this kind of restlessness or difficulty sitting still back when you were a child or teenager, or is this something that's only started more recently in your life?

Oh, well... I suppose it's not entirely new. I really hate to admit this, because I always try to be respectful and follow the rules, you know? But... um... back when I was just a little guy in grade school, I guess I did get into a bit of trouble sometimes. 

Nothing malicious, I promise! Just... well, I had a bad habit of popping out of my seat when I wasn't supposed to. And, um, sometimes I'd accidentally talk over the teacher, or I'd just start rushing ahead on my assignments before they even finished giving us the directions. I just had so much energy I didn't know what to do with it. My mother, she used to always sigh and say I acted like I was just... wound too tight, even as a kid. 

Does that answer your question, Doctor? I hope I'm not making myself sound like a terrible student or a bad kid, I really did try my best to be good.

When you're feeling that 'motor humming' and needing to move, is it usually paired with a lot of worried or anxious thoughts running through your mind, or is it more just a physical urge to move without much worrying attached to it?

Oh, um... that's a really good question, Doctor. Let me think about that so I can give you the right answer. 

I guess... I wouldn't really say it's because I'm worried or anxious about anything. I don't want you to think I'm sitting there fretting or stressing out about my job or life, I really try to just count my blessings and stay cheerful. 

It's more just... well, just like you said, a physical urge. It's just my body feeling like it needs to be doing something, rather than my mind spinning with bad thoughts. I hope that makes sense? I just want to be sure I'm explaining it clearly so I'm not wasting your time. Is that the kind of information you were looking for?

latest_inference.note: Patient reports childhood-onset hyperactivity/impulsivity (fidgeting, blurting out, rushing through tasks) persisting into adulthood, and denies anxious/worried thoughts accompanying the restlessness, making it physical/motor rather than cognitive-anxiety driven. This effectively rules out F41.1 (GAD), which requires prominent worry, and supports a chronic neurodevelopmental pattern consistent with ADHD.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports chronic, pervasive motor restlessness ('little motor humming'), difficulty remaining seated during meetings, need to get up and move, and impulsive behaviors (blurting out, rushing through tasks) that began in childhood (grade school) and have persisted into adulthood, causing functional difficulty in occupational/social settings (staff meetings, church briefings). Symptoms are described as a physical urge to move rather than being driven by anxious cognitions, and no new medications or substances could account for the restlessness, ruling out medication-induced akathisia or an anxiety disorder. The childhood onset, chronic course, and hyperactive-impulsive symptom pattern without a primary mood or anxiety component support a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation (F90.0).
